cls: Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (nutritional supplement)
pharm: An omega-3 (n-3) long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid that is a major structural lipid of neural and retinal membranes; it modulates membrane fluidity and serves as a precursor for anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving lipid mediators (resolvins, protectins) and influences triglyceride metabolism.

summary: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is an omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid found in oily fish and algal oil and is marketed as a nutritional/dietary supplement (often with eicosapentaenoic acid, EPA). It is a key structural component of the brain (especially gray matter) and the retina, and is widely supplemented during pregnancy and lactation to support fetal and infant neural and visual development. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA + DHA) also lower elevated serum triglycerides and have anti-inflammatory/pro-resolving effects. As a supplement, DHA is generally well tolerated; the most common effects are mild gastrointestinal upset, a fishy aftertaste/eructation, and, at high doses, a modest increase in bleeding tendency. It is not an FDA-approved drug as DHA alone; prescription omega-3 products (e.g. icosapent ethyl, omega-3-acid ethyl esters) are FDA-approved for severe hypertriglyceridemia, but DHA on its own is a supplement, so this record is sourced from EMA/SmPC and BNF-type guidance.
indications: Dietary supplementation of omega-3 fatty acids, including to support fetal and infant brain and eye (retinal) development during pregnancy and lactation
Adjunct (as part of EPA+DHA omega-3 preparations) to diet for reduction of elevated serum triglycerides (note: prescription omega-3 acid products carry this approved use, not DHA alone)

moa: DHA is incorporated into cell membrane phospholipids, where it is especially concentrated in neuronal synaptic membranes and retinal photoreceptors, contributing to membrane fluidity, signaling, and visual and neural function. As an omega-3 fatty acid it competes with arachidonic acid (omega-6) as an enzyme substrate, shifting eicosanoid production toward less inflammatory mediators and serving as a precursor for specialized pro-resolving mediators (resolvins and protectins) that help resolve inflammation. Omega-3 fatty acids also reduce hepatic synthesis and secretion of triglycerides (very-low-density lipoprotein) and enhance triglyceride clearance, accounting for their triglyceride-lowering effect.

preg: DHA is widely recommended during pregnancy to support fetal brain and retinal development, with intakes around 200-300 mg/day commonly advised. It is considered safe at supplemental doses; very high-dose fish-oil products should be used with attention to contaminant content. Follow obstetric and dietary guidance.
lact: DHA is secreted into breast milk and supports infant neurodevelopment; maternal supplementation is recommended to maintain adequate milk DHA. It is considered safe during breastfeeding at supplemental doses.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for renal impairment when DHA is used as a supplement.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment when DHA is used as a supplement; monitor lipids if used therapeutically.

moderate: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents (e.g. warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) - high-dose omega-3 may modestly prolong bleeding time; monitor for bleeding
minor: Antihypertensives - omega-3 may have a small additive blood-pressure-lowering effect
interactions.food: Take with food to improve absorption and tolerability.
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; note that alcohol independently raises triglycerides, which may offset triglyceride-lowering use.
interactions.diagnostics: High doses may slightly prolong bleeding time; monitor INR if on warfarin. May modestly raise LDL cholesterol in some patients.

serious: Increased bleeding tendency at high doses
Allergic reaction in fish-allergic individuals (fish-oil products)
rare: Atrial fibrillation reported with high-dose prescription omega-3 in some studies

Signs of bleeding, especially with anticoagulants or before surgery (high doses)

counsel: DHA is an omega-3 fatty acid found in fish and algae oil that supports brain and eye health
Take it with a meal to absorb it better and reduce fishy burps; refrigerating the capsules can help too
During pregnancy and breastfeeding it helps your baby's brain and eye development - take the amount your clinician recommends
If you take blood thinners or are due for surgery, tell your doctor, as high doses can slightly increase bleeding
If you are allergic to fish, choose an algae-based DHA product
It is a supplement, not a substitute for prescribed medicines or a healthy diet
pk: Incorporated into membranes gradually over weeks of regular intake
Plasma fatty-acid levels rise within hours of a dose; tissue levels build over weeks
Long tissue residence as a structural membrane lipid
Sustained with daily intake; benefits accrue with continued use
Store cool and dry, away from light; refrigeration can reduce fishy aftertaste and oxidation
pearls: DHA is a SUPPLEMENT, not an FDA-approved single-agent drug - information here follows EMA/SmPC and BNF-type guidance (prescription omega-3 products for hypertriglyceridemia are EPA+DHA combinations or icosapent ethyl)
Major structural lipid of the brain and retina - supplemented in pregnancy/lactation (~200-300 mg/day) for fetal/infant neurodevelopment
Omega-3s lower elevated triglycerides but may slightly raise LDL cholesterol
High doses can modestly increase bleeding - caution with anticoagulants and before surgery
Fishy aftertaste/burping is the most common complaint - take with food and refrigerate capsules
Algal-oil DHA is a vegetarian/fish-allergy-safe alternative to fish-oil DHA
missed: If you miss a dose of your DHA supplement, take it when you remember, or skip it and resume your normal schedule if it is almost time for the next dose. Do not double up. Consistent daily intake matters more than any single dose.
overdose: DHA has a wide safety margin. Excessive intake mainly causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea) and, at very high doses, an increased tendency to bleed. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive - reduce or stop the supplement and watch for bleeding in those on anticoagulants.
